cat > docs/zig-rewrite.md <<'EOF'
# Zig 0.17.0 rewrite experiment

This branch contains a standalone implementation of jbsync in Zig. `zig build`
produces `zig-out/bin/jbsync` (on Windows, `jbsync.exe`), without invoking Rust
or linking its runtime. The Rust source and existing release workflows remain
available to compare behavior before deciding whether to replace them.

The scaffolding was generated with the installed **`zig init`**, then adapted
for this application. The package fingerprint is the one generated by Zig.
Development follows the [Zig 0.17.0 language reference](https://ziglang.org/documentation/0.17.0/)
and the installed toolchain's standard-library source.

## Build and test

Install/use Zig 0.17.0, Git, and Python 3 for the CLI fixtures:

```sh
zig version                        # 0.17.0
zig build                          # Debug binary
zig build test --summary all        # library tests
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe
python3 tests/zig/integration.py zig-out/bin/jbsync
zig build run -- --help
```

On Windows, pass `zig-out/bin/jbsync.exe` to the Python script. If the default
Zig cache is inaccessible, set `ZIG_GLOBAL_CACHE_DIR` to a writable directory.
`mise run zig-ci` performs the same checks. The original Rust tasks still work.

`.github/workflows/zig.yml` runs native tests on macOS, Linux and Windows and
cross-compiles macOS ARM64/Intel, Linux ARM64/AMD64, and Windows AMD64 binaries.
The workflow uploads experimental binaries as artifacts; it does not publish
releases or change the installers.

All CLI scenarios create temporary IDE directories and Git repositories. They
never point at the user's actual JetBrains settings or call real IDE launchers.

## Design

- `src/root.zig` exports the library; `src/main.zig` owns process initialization,
  output, and the process-lifetime arena. Every allocating library operation
  takes the caller's allocator explicitly. Trees, projections, configuration,
  and planned writes live in that arena. Tests release the arena with `defer`.
- `std.process.Init` supplies `std.Io`, arguments and the environment. Filesystem
  and child-process operations receive the I/O context explicitly. There is no
  libc binding or third-party Zig package. Git transports store history; the OS
  hostname utility supplies the default identity when environment variables do
  not provide it.
- `xml.zig` holds ordered children and deterministic sorted attributes, decodes
  entities, handles CDATA and rejects malformed or ambiguous projections.
  Domain elements with no value attribute are represented by their existence.
  Address delimiters inside identifiers are escaped. Incoming ordered children
  are applied in donor document order, including indices above nine.
- `merge.zig` performs pure three-way reconciliation of XML leaves, JVM flags,
  and opaque store metadata. It returns explicit changes and conflicts.
- `config.zig` reads the TOML forms used by jbsync's configuration and saved
  defaults. `settings.zig` handles discovery, manifests, pruning, product
  metadata, exclusions, and product-specific VM options names. Roaming policy
  data is carried forward from the Rust implementation in `policy.zig`.
- `engine.zig` converges the IDEs through up to four passes. All file changes
  are planned in memory, so `--prefer neither` can abort before applying any
  settings, store, backup, or baseline writes. Dry runs use those same staged
  views. Remote sync policy takes effect within the same run.
- `files.zig` checks paths below trusted roots, refuses symlink settings paths,
  writes and syncs a temporary file before atomic replacement, and takes an OS
  advisory lock around a sync. Backups are saved before originals change and
  preserve pre-run bytes even across multiple convergence passes. Ten backup
  runs are retained. The application directory is private on POSIX.
- `git.zig` reconciles file trees structurally before recording the remote as
  an `ours` merge parent. It distinguishes an empty remote from fetch failures,
  retries publishing even when no new commit is needed, and preserves binary
  bytes using the same `* -text` store attributes as Rust.
- `plugins.zig` uses `std.zip` to read JAR descriptors, writes the compatible
  JSON manifest, checks build ranges/modules/incompatibilities and scoped
  rules, and plans managed dependencies before their dependents. IDE launchers
  run only after conflict validation. Plugin directories are never copied.

## Tested behavior

The Zig library suite covers canonical XML, entities, child order, named domain
presence, escaped addresses, disjoint edits, conflicts and policies, deletions,
JVM flags, configuration layering, pruning, numeric builds, glob selectors,
plugin descriptors and compatibility, and twelve-item ordered lists.

The CLI suite covers:

- multiple IDEs contributing disjoint edits, convergence, backups and idempotence;
- second-machine adoption, divergent Git histories, and two-machine disjoint edits;
- conflict policy and `neither` leaving all settings bytes unchanged;
- dry-run snapshots and plans matching the subsequent sync;
- privacy pruning with surgical preservation of unshared IDE content;
- incoming exclusions and machine overrides;
- unlaunched IDE factory defaults and launch gating;
- compressed JAR descriptors, plugin manifests and idempotent rule commands;
- product-specific VM options and collect-only followed by a full sync;
- deletion propagation, lock contention, symlink rejection, invalid config,
  command-specific flags, and builtin sync switches.

Lock/symlink fixtures use POSIX facilities and are skipped on Windows; native
Windows CI still exercises the remaining scenarios. Cross-compilation is not
proof of native execution; see the PR checks for platform results.

A local comparison using the existing cached Rust debug binary passed eight
of the initial ten scenarios. Its two differences were argument-error exit
status (Rust uses 2) and `--prefer neither` (the cached binary writes settings
and exits successfully). The Zig fixture deliberately requires a nonzero exit
and no settings writes for unresolved conflicts. That cached binary is not a
fresh rebuild of the retained Rust source and is not a complete parity audit.

## Remaining parity and release work

This is an experiment for review and testing, not a release migration:

- **Self-update is unavailable.** Current releases contain Rust binaries. The
  Zig `update` command explains this and exits unsuccessfully rather than
  replacing the experiment with a Rust binary. Installer/release packaging and
  checksum-verified replacement need a separate validation step.
- **TOML is a documented subset.** Basic/literal strings, booleans, integers,
  arrays (including multiline arrays), ordinary/dotted/quoted tables, arrays
  of tables and inline maps are supported. Multiline strings, floats and dates
  are rejected. This is not a general TOML 1.0 parser; configuration using
  unsupported syntax must be simplified or the parser replaced before rollout.
- Shell completions cover top-level commands. The Rust completion output and
  terminal styling/progress/report layout have not been replicated exactly.
- Lossless XML equivalence has fixture coverage; a full real-installation
  corpus comparison remains outstanding. Mixed-content XML is unsupported by
  the structured DOM and stays opaque; DTD/entity definitions are unsupported.
- Actual Marketplace downloads, running IDE reload behavior, and installation
  metadata discovery across real Toolbox layouts need live validation.
- Library callers provide an arena whose lifetime covers their entire operation.
  Allocations are bounded per file/descriptor, but total peak memory and speed
  have not been benchmarked against Rust on large installations.

For an isolated manual trial, use a dedicated `--config-dir`, a copied IDE
configuration root, and a disposable Git remote. Start with `status` or
`sync --dry-run --no-install-plugins` before applying a plan.
EOF
ZIG_GLOBAL_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/jbsync-zig-cache zig fmt src && ZIG_GLOBAL_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/jbsync-zig-cache zig build test --summary all && ZIG_GLOBAL_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/jbsync-zig-cache zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe && python3 tests/zig/integration.py zig-out/bin/jbsync",yield_time_ms:1000,max_output_tokens:1500}));

**Analyzing Git initialization**

I'm considering the `Git.initialize` optional parameter which dictates whether to adopt a remote or not. It seems like if the `adopt` parameter is set to true, the procedure creates attributes even before the snapshot, but the `.gitattributes` settings remain empty initially. I’m aware of the complexities such as managing several attributes—committing changes without actually staging content. The use of `merge-base` also adds some layers to this process. Overall, the logic behind the initialization process needs clarity to ensure all conditions are appropriately handled.

**Addressing symlink errors**

I'm working through an issue with symlink errors when dealing with shared attributes. It looks like fixing the `.shared` local setting should allow the project to adopt correctly. The `.writeBack` function starts with raw, pruned settings from the donor. There's a need for the registry to preserve the full filename, especially for the `.ide.general.xml` manifest. I’m also considering the launch marker. If this factory IDE has a registry, that marker should reflect the original state too, to keep everything aligned.

payload.input:
text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > /tmp/jbsync-zig-pr-body.md <<'EOF'
Adds a standalone Zig 0.17.0 implementation of jbsync so the project can be tested with a Zig toolchain before replacing the Rust implementation. `zig build` produces the CLI without Rust or third-party Zig packages. Rust and the existing release pipeline remain as the comparison baseline.

The package/build/library/CLI scaffolding was generated with the installed `zig init`. The rewrite uses explicit caller allocators, a process-lifetime arena, `std.process.Init` / `std.Io`, native build modules and tests, and `std.zip` for JAR descriptors, following https://ziglang.org/documentation/0.17.0/ and the installed standard library.

### Behavior

Implements IDE/product discovery, learned roaming manifests and factory defaults, privacy/default pruning and layered omit rules, leaf-level XML and JVM-flag three-way merges, multi-IDE convergence, Git tree reconciliation, atomic writes, pre-run backups, OS advisory locking, plugin manifests/compatibility/rules/dependency ordering, builtin sync switches, and command completions.

`--prefer neither` validates the complete plan before any settings are applied. Dry runs use staged views throughout the reconciliation. Collect-only records what the IDE actually contributed, so a subsequent full sync can still adopt incoming settings. XML applies ordered additions in donor order and represents named domain elements by their presence. Unsafe relative paths and local symlinks are rejected.

### Validation

- Installed Zig reports **0.17.0**.
- `zig build test --summary all`: **11 tests passed**.
- `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe`: passed on native macOS ARM64.
- `python3 tests/zig/integration.py zig-out/bin/jbsync`: **14 CLI/Git scenarios passed** using disposable IDE roots and bare remotes. No actual IDE settings were used or Marketplace downloads invoked.
- ReleaseSafe cross-compilation: Linux AMD64/ARM64, macOS Intel, Windows AMD64.
- Zig formatting and `git diff --check`: passed.
- New CI runs native builds/tests on macOS, Linux and Windows, cross-compiles five targets, and uploads experimental binaries. POSIX lock/symlink fixtures are skipped on Windows.

A comparison run against the existing cached Rust debug binary passed eight of the initial ten scenarios. Its differences were invalid-option exit status and writing settings under `--prefer neither`. This was not a fresh Rust build or a complete differential audit.

### Draft limitations

Self-update is explicitly unavailable until Zig release packaging and checksum-verified replacement are validated. The TOML reader supports jbsync's common configuration forms but rejects multiline strings, floats and dates; it is not a general TOML 1.0 implementation. Completion/report presentation is simpler than Rust. Full real-installation XML corpus parity, actual Marketplace installation, real Toolbox discovery, and memory/performance benchmarks remain outstanding.

See [the experiment guide](docs/zig-rewrite.md) for architecture, test coverage, isolated trial instructions and the remaining migration work. This PR does not switch release installers to the experimental binary.
EOF

cat > /tmp/jbsync-zig-pr-body.md <<'EOF'
Adds a standalone Zig 0.17.0 implementation of jbsync so the project can be tested with a Zig toolchain before replacing the Rust implementation. `zig build` produces the CLI without Rust or third-party Zig packages. Rust and the existing release pipeline remain as the comparison baseline.

The package/build/library/CLI scaffolding was generated with the installed `zig init`. The rewrite uses explicit caller allocators, a process-lifetime arena, `std.process.Init` / `std.Io`, native build modules and tests, and `std.zip` for JAR descriptors, following https://ziglang.org/documentation/0.17.0/ and the installed standard library.

### Behavior

Implements IDE/product discovery, learned roaming manifests and factory defaults, privacy/default pruning and layered omit rules, leaf-level XML and JVM-flag three-way merges, multi-IDE convergence, Git tree reconciliation, atomic writes, pre-run backups, OS advisory locking, plugin manifests/compatibility/rules/dependency ordering, builtin sync switches, and command completions.

`--prefer neither` validates the complete plan before any settings are applied. Dry runs use staged views throughout the reconciliation. Collect-only records what the IDE actually contributed, so a subsequent full sync can still adopt incoming settings. XML applies ordered additions in donor order and represents named domain elements by their presence. Unsafe relative paths and local symlinks are rejected.

### Validation

- Installed Zig reports **0.17.0**.
- `zig build test --summary all`: **11 tests passed**.
- `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe`: passed on native macOS ARM64.
- `python3 tests/zig/integration.py zig-out/bin/jbsync`: **14 CLI/Git scenarios passed** using disposable IDE roots and bare remotes. No actual IDE settings were used or Marketplace downloads invoked.
- ReleaseSafe cross-compilation: Linux AMD64/ARM64, macOS Intel, Windows AMD64.
- Zig formatting and `git diff --check`: passed.
- New CI runs native builds/tests on macOS, Linux and Windows, cross-compiles five targets, and uploads experimental binaries. POSIX lock/symlink fixtures are skipped on Windows.

A comparison run against the existing cached Rust debug binary passed eight of the initial ten scenarios. Its differences were invalid-option exit status and writing settings under `--prefer neither`. This was not a fresh Rust build or a complete differential audit.

### Draft limitations

Self-update is explicitly unavailable until Zig release packaging and checksum-verified replacement are validated. The TOML reader supports jbsync's common configuration forms but rejects multiline strings, floats and dates; it is not a general TOML 1.0 implementation. Completion/report presentation is simpler than Rust. Full real-installation XML corpus parity, actual Marketplace installation, real Toolbox discovery, and memory/performance benchmarks remain outstanding.

See [the experiment guide](docs/zig-rewrite.md) for architecture, test coverage, isolated trial instructions and the remaining migration work. This PR does not switch release installers to the experimental binary.
EOF
git push -u origin codex/zig-0.17-rewrite && gh pr create --draft --base main --head codex/zig-0.17-rewrite --title "Experiment: rewrite jbsync in Zig 0.17.0" --body-file /tmp/jbsync-zig-pr-body.md

        project::project(&reparsed),

and platform checks. The Rust tasks remain available.

```sh
cargo build --locked --example validation_oracle
zig build validation -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe
python3 tests/zig/differential.py zig-out/bin/jbsync-validation target/debug/examples/validation_oracle
cargo build --locked --release
python3 tests/zig/integration.py target/release/jbsync --rust-baseline
python3 tests/zig/benchmark.py zig-out/bin/jbsync target/release/jbsync
sh tests/zig/platform.sh
```

`.github/workflows/zig.yml` runs the same validation on Apple Silicon macOS
in Debug, ReleaseSafe and ReleaseFast modes. It uploads each experimental
binary. The Rust workflow runs its complete original suite, formatting, Clippy
and the shared CLI scenarios. No Intel Mac, Linux or Windows artifacts are built.
The previous Windows failure was CRLF checkout formatting; `.gitattributes`
now enforces LF. The failing Linux runtime job was removed with Linux support;
its `Unexpected` runtime failure was not diagnosed or claimed as repaired.

''' +s[end:];s=s.replace('handles CDATA and rejects malformed or ambiguous projections.', 'handles CDATA and rejects malformed projections. Replacement preserves existing file permissions.');s=s.replace('The application directory is private on POSIX.', 'The application directory is private. Staged disk reads and directory lists are\n  cached per sync; no-op writes are dropped. Before committing, every planned\n  destination is rechecked for symlinks and concurrent edits. Git internals and\n  excluded IDE caches are skipped during traversal.');s=s.replace('and plans managed dependencies before their dependents.', 'and plans managed dependencies before their dependents. Capabilities do not\n  imply installation; bundled IDs and actual plugin presence are tracked\n  separately. permission preservation, real XML corpus convergence and subsequent edits,
plugin launchers simulated with a local executable, capability/bundled decisions,
managed plugin dependencies, failed fetches, selectors and immediate remote policy.

The differential suite makes **2,688 deterministic comparisons** with a freshly
built Rust oracle: all 14 real XML fixtures, Unicode/entities/attribute whitespace,
1,500 generated XML merges across all policies, 192 add/delete/tombstone cases,
450 JVM option merges, glob cases and 320 plugin compatibility combinations.
It compares semantic XML with ordered children rather than attribute order.
The native suite also injects allocation failures and tests concurrent-edit
preflight checks, parser depth limits and malformed XML.

The fresh Rust baseline passed its 143 active tests (one optional live-corpus
test is ignored). The shared CLI runner's `--rust-baseline` mode exercises 19
matching scenarios and explicitly skips seven known differences: Rust writes
under `--prefer neither`, coalesces rapid backups by second, suppresses failed
fetches, skips symlinks rather than rejecting the sync, loses edits to repeated
IntelliLang addresses, retains a deleted shared file in the other machine, and
applies incoming policy on the next run. Zig's stricter checks remain enabled.
Argument errors use exit status 2 in Rust and 1 in Zig.

The benchmark creates two disposable IDEs with 200 settings files, 4,000 leaves
and 2,000 excluded cache files, then times five settled syncs. Local ReleaseSafe
medians were 60.2 ms after optimization, 70.5 ms before, and 67.3 ms for Rust
release (about 15% faster than the original Zig version). These local results
include Git/process overhead, are workload-specific and are not CI thresholds.
No claim is made about Marketplace performance or live IDE behavior.

''' +s[end:];s=s.replace('Installer/release packaging and\n  checksum-verified replacement need a separate validation step.', 'Release packaging remains Rust-based until the experiment is accepted.\n  The narrowed installer retains checksum/version verification and atomic\n  installation; Zig self-replacement needs separate implementation/validation.');s=s.replace('a full real-installation\n  corpus comparison remains outstanding.', 'the committed 14-file real-world\n  corpus is compared with Rust; a fresh live-installation scan remains outstanding.');s=s.replace('Allocations are bounded per file/descriptor, but total peak memory and speed\n  have not been benchmarked against Rust on large installations.', 'Allocations are bounded per file/descriptor. A synthetic speed benchmark is\n  included; peak memory on large live installations remains unmeasured.');p.write_text(s)
p=Path('mise.toml');s=p.read_text().replace('zig fmt --check build.zig build.zig.zon src/main.zig src/root.zig src/zig', 'zig fmt --check build.zig build.zig.zon src');s=s.replace('run = ["zig fmt --check build.zig build.zig.zon src", "zig build test", "zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe", "python3 tests/zig/integration.py zig-out/bin/jbsync"]', 'run = ["zig fmt --check build.zig build.zig.zon src", "zig build test --summary all -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe", "zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe", "zig build validation -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe", "cargo build --locked --example validation_oracle", "python3 tests/zig/integration.py zig-out/bin/jbsync", "python3 tests/zig/differential.py zig-out/bin/jbsync-validation target/debug/examples/validation_oracle", "sh tests/zig/platform.sh"]');p.write_text(s)

## Plugins

`jbsync` records which third-party plugins you have in `plugins.json`, together
with the compatibility metadata from each descriptor, and other machines install
them from Marketplace through the IDE's own launcher.

Plugin directories are never copied. They contain compiled code and sometimes
native libraries, so copying them between machines — or between macOS and
Windows — is unsound.

Compatibility is checked before anything is installed: build ranges, required
modules, and `incompatible-with` declarations. A Python-only plugin is not
offered to CLion. `jbsync plugins` shows the manifest and the verdict per IDE;
a sync installs what is missing, and `--no-install-plugins` reduces that to a
report.
trait — only Convex offers real push, so it belongs in a separate opt-in
capability rather than forcing every backend to fake one. `repo.backend` in
`config.toml` already selects the implementation.

### Why Git is a subprocess

jbsync runs the `git` binary rather than linking a Git library. That keeps
authentication as whatever already works for you — SSH agent, Keychain, Windows
Credential Manager, `gh auth`, hardware keys — instead of reimplementing it, and
avoids a C dependency in every one of eight release targets.

When another machine has published since this one last looked, jbsync merges
semantically and then records the remote as a parent, so history stays honest
without Git's line merge ever touching a settings file.

## 6. Plugins

jbsync records which third-party plugins you have in `plugins.json`, with the
compatibility metadata from each descriptor. Other machines install them from
Marketplace through the IDE's own launcher.

**Plugin directories are never copied.** They contain compiled code and
sometimes native libraries; copying them between machines — let alone between
macOS and Windows — is unsound.

Compatibility is checked before anything is installed: build ranges (including
`.*` wildcards), required modules against what each IDE provides, and
`incompatible-with` declarations. A Python-only plugin is not offered to CLion.
```toml
# sync.toml
[jetbrains]
exclude = ["options/sshConfigs.xml", "options/github.xml"]
```

Authentication is whatever already works for you — SSH agent, macOS Keychain,
Windows Credential Manager, `gh auth`, a hardware key. jbsync runs the `git`
you have installed rather than embedding its own client, so there are no
separate credentials to configure.
